topics: 💰 Etnan Zonah — payment to a prostitute is barred from the altar
🐕 Mechir Kelev — an animal exchanged for a dog is likewise barred
🔢 'Both of Them' — two categories are prohibited, not four
🐑 Nineteen Lambs and a Dog — how partners dividing property spoil ten lambs
🌾 Wheat Into Flour — Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on whether change permits

overview.title: 📖 Overview: What May Not Come Onto the Altar
overview.subtitle: Temurah 30a–30b
overview.hebrewSource: לֹא תָבִיא אֶתְנַן זוֹנָה וּמְחִיר כֶּלֶב בֵּית ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ לְכׇל נֶדֶר — כִּי תוֹעֲבַת ה׳ אֱלֹהֶיךָ גַּם שְׁנֵיהֶם
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Deuteronomy 23:19 bars two things from the Temple: etnan zonah, an animal given to a prostitute as her fee, and mechir kelev, an animal given in exchange for a dog. The daf works out the precise boundaries of both. It asks who counts as a prostitute, whether 'price' means money or barter, how the ban spreads when a dog is bundled into a division of property, and — the chapter's sharpest question — whether grinding the wheat into flour launders it. Along the way it settles what happens to the offspring of a disqualified animal and even to its dung.

slides.title: 👰 Is a Widow Paid by a High Priest an 'Etnan'?
slides.subtitle: Why the baraita chose that case rather than the obvious one

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: The baraita follows Rabbi Elazar, who holds that an unmarried man who has relations with an unmarried woman not for marriage has made her a prostitute — so her fee is barred.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But if so, why cite the widow paid by a High Priest? Let it simply teach the unmarried case, which is the paradigm!

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: Precisely because you might have reasoned the opposite way: the unmarried case is only a rabbinic-level impropriety, so that is where the ban belongs; but where the union is forbidden by Torah law, perhaps the fee is too remote to be called an etnan.

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: So the baraita teaches the harder case: even a Torah-forbidden union — a High Priest with a widow — produces an etnan that may not come onto the altar.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: Abaye, by contrast, holds like the Rabbis, who disagree with Rabbi Elazar about the unmarried couple entirely.

callout.label: Principle:
callout.text: The prohibition tracks the payment, not the severity of the sin — a forbidden relationship does not exempt the fee.

slides.title: 🐑 Nineteen Lambs and One Dog
slides.subtitle: The mishna's case of two partners dividing their common property

nodes.content: 🤝 Partners hold 19 lambs and 1 dog in common, then divide

columns.label: Partner A
columns.content: Takes 10 lambs — received in exchange for the other's 9 lambs and the dog

columns.label: Partner B
columns.content: Takes 9 lambs + the dog — nothing was exchanged for a dog

nodes.content: ❓ Why are all ten barred? Just set one lamb aside against the dog and the other nine are clean!
💡 The case is where the dog is worth more than any single lamb. No one lamb can absorb it, so the dog's value is spread across all ten — and every one of them is tainted.

callout.label: Note:
callout.text: 'Price' (מְחִיר) here means an item bartered, not money — proven from Psalms 44:13, 'You sell Your people without wealth, and have not set their prices high.'

slides.title: 🔢 'Both of Them' — Two Are Barred, Not Four
slides.subtitle: The verse names exactly two categories, and the count is doing real work
rows: A lamb given to a prostitute as her fee
A lamb given in exchange for a dog
A lamb paid for relations with one's dog
There is no 'prostitution' with an animal
A lamb paid as the price of a prostitute, to buy her as a maidservant
That is a purchase price, not a fee for services
The offspring of a barred animal

callout.label: The derivation:
callout.text: Had the verse meant only two loosely, it could have written 'the payment of a prostitute or a dog'. Writing payment of one and price of the other shows they are two distinct mechanisms — and 'both of them' caps the list at two.

slides.title: 🌾 Does Physical Change Launder the Payment?
slides.subtitle: He gave her wheat and she milled it; olives and she pressed them; grapes and she made wine

boxes.title: Beit Hillel — Permitted
items: The milling makes a new object, outside the ban
Difficulty: they have no good reading of the word 'even' (גַּם)

boxes.title: Beit Shammai — Prohibited
items: They too derive 'them, but not their offspring'
But the extra word 'even' (גַּם) includes the changed form
Flour, oil and wine stay barred

boxes.title: Two Other Readings of the Verse
items: Rabbi Elazar: 'into the House of the Lord' excludes the red heifer, slaughtered outside on the Mount of Olives
The Rabbis: it includes beaten gold plates for the Temple
Rabbi Yosei bar Yehuda: not even for the space behind the Ark Cover

callout.label: Rav Yosef's source:
callout.text: Guryon of Aspork taught the baraita as an explicit Beit Shammai / Beit Hillel dispute, which resolves the two contradictory baraitot.

slides.title: 🍼 How Far Does the Taint Spread?
slides.subtitle: Offspring, dung, and the fetus in the womb

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rava: an animal that was the object of bestiality while pregnant — its offspring is barred too, as though mother and young were both used
2️⃣ Same for a pregnant cow that gored and killed — it is as if both gored
3️⃣ But offspring of a set-aside or idol-worshipped animal are permitted: only the mother was set aside or worshipped (a second version reverses this — the extra girth benefits the owner)
4️⃣ Rav Aḥadevoi bar Ami in Rav's name: betrothal with the dung of a stoned ox works; with the dung of idolatrous calves it does not
5️⃣ Why? Extra girth flatters an idol's calf, so its dung is part of the offering ('anything you produce from it'); a stoned ox gains its owner nothing, and only 'its flesh' is forbidden (Ex. 21:28)

callout.label: The mishna's dispute:
callout.text: Rabbi Eliezer bars the offspring of a tereifa; Rabbi Ḥanina ben Antigonus disqualifies even a kosher animal that suckled from one. Rav Naḥman and Rava then argue over exactly which case Rabbi Eliezer and the Rabbis are fighting about — conceived-then-used, or used-then-conceived.

summary.principle: Deuteronomy 23:19 bars exactly two things from the altar — a prostitute's fee and an animal bartered for a dog — and the daf polices both the outer edge of that list and how far the disqualification travels.

flowSteps.content: 📜 'You shall not bring the payment of a prostitute or the price of a dog… for both of them are an abomination'
🔢 'Both of them' = two categories, not four → payment for relations with a dog, and the price paid for a prostitute herself, are permitted

columns.content: 🐑 Dog worth more than any one lamb → its value spreads over all ten, barring them all
🌾 Wheat milled into flour → Beit Hillel permit ('them, not their changed form'), Beit Shammai bar it ('even')

flowSteps.content: 🍼 Offspring generally permitted — except where mother and fetus are treated as one, as in bestiality or goring during pregnancy
🎓 Key Principle: a consecrated animal cannot become an etnan — 'for any vow' excludes it, since one cannot prohibit what is not his

quiz.q: According to the mishna, which of these IS permitted to be sacrificed on the altar?
o: A lamb given to a prostitute as her fee
A lamb given in exchange for a dog
A lamb given as the price to purchase a prostitute as a maidservant
Flour a prostitute milled from wheat she was paid, according to Beit Shammai
quiz.e: The verse's 'both of them' limits the ban to two categories. Payment for relations with a dog, and the purchase price of a prostitute herself, fall outside it and are permitted.

quiz.q: Why are all ten lambs barred when partners split nineteen lambs and a dog?
o: Because a dog can never be owned in partnership
Because the dog is worth more than any single lamb, so its value is spread across all ten
Because the Rabbis penalized the partner who took the larger share
Because the lambs were consecrated before the division
quiz.e: If one lamb could be set aside against the dog, the other nine would be clean. The Gemara answers that the case is where the dog outvalues each individual lamb, so no single lamb absorbs it.

quiz.q: What is the dispute between Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel on this daf?
o: Whether a widow paid by a High Priest creates an etnan
Whether the offspring of a tereifa may be sacrificed
Whether payment that has physically changed form — wheat milled into flour — remains barred
Whether 'price' in the verse means money or barter
quiz.e: Beit Hillel read 'them' to exclude the changed form and permit the flour, oil or wine; Beit Shammai read the extra word 'even' as including it. Rav Yosef cites Guryon of Aspork for this attribution.

quiz.q: Why may one betroth a woman with the dung of an ox sentenced to stoning, but not with the dung of calves used for idol worship?
o: The stoned ox's dung is worth less than a peruta
Extra girth flatters an idolatrous calf so its dung is part of the offering, while a stoned ox's girth benefits its owner not at all
Idolatrous calves are never actually stoned
Dung is always permitted; the case concerns the animals themselves
quiz.e: The Gemara gives both a logical reason (the owner gains from a fatter idol, not from a fatter condemned ox) and a scriptural one ('anything you produce from it' for idolatry, versus 'its flesh shall not be eaten' for the stoned ox).

quiz.q: How can a consecrated animal ever become an etnan, given that one cannot prohibit what is not his?
o: It cannot, under any circumstance
Rav Hoshaya: where he registers the prostitute for his Paschal offering, following Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi that a Paschal offering counts as personal property for registration
Where the animal was consecrated after being given to her
Where the owner later redeems the animal
quiz.e: Rav Hoshaya explains the case as registering her for a share in his Paschal offering. Rabbi Yehuda HaNasi holds one may 'sustain himself from the lamb', so the money received for registering others is non-sacred and the transaction is his to make.
